referents.why: First person 'me' inside Pharaoh's speech (the speech opened by the frame cl1). The speaker is Pharaoh, the masculine singular candidate w2.
'my people' is the speaker's possessive inside Pharaoh's speech, so the referent is the speaker, Pharaoh (w2).
'he said' is a wayyiqtol in the narrative frame. Its subject is the one who summoned Moses and Aaron in cl0, Pharaoh (w2), masculine singular.
referents.category: narrative subject carried from the frame

referents.why: The imperative 'pray' is spoken to Moses and Aaron together. Second person masculine plural matches the composite c3 (two men).
referents.category: implied you of a command to two

referents.why: The jussive 'that he may remove the frogs' is the purpose of the prayer in cl2, so its subject is the LORD prayed to. w12 and w31 are both the LORD in this verse; w12 is the one the prayer names. Masculine singular agrees.
referents.category: implied subject of a purpose clause after a prayer

referents.why: First person 'I will let go' inside Pharaoh's speech: the speaker, Pharaoh (w2).

'that they may sacrifice' states the purpose of letting go the people in cl4, so 'they' is the people released. w27 is that people. The noun is grammatically masculine singular but a collective, which takes plural agreement by sense.
referents.category: plural pronoun for a collective noun

links.why: Reverses the narrative order. The wayyiqtol cl1 continues from the nearest earlier clause, cl0 (summoned), so the link runs cl0 then cl1, not cl1 then cl0.
Wayyiqtol cl1 continues the narrative line from cl0, the nearest earlier clause that is not inside a speech.
The waw joins an imperative (second person) to a jussive in the third person. The rule for a command joined to a change of person is 'so that', not a plain 'and'.
links.category: command then jussive in a different person

links.why: Pray, and so that he may remove the frogs: waw plus a jussive in a different person after a command is a purpose. The sense agrees: the prayer is for the removal.

A plain waw joins a jussive to a cohortative. A cohortative after a jussive is a promise, not a purpose, and the form marks no condition, so the plain 'and' stands. Whether the promise is conditional on the removal is left to cant_tell.
The waw joins a first-person act to a jussive in the third person. The release is plainly for the sacrifice, so the link is a purpose, not a plain 'and'.

I will let the people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD. The sense requires purpose and the form is waw plus a jussive in a different person. The exception for a cohortative after a jussive does not apply, because here the cohortative comes first.

groups.why: Pharaoh's speech to Moses and Aaron. The builder put slot ids where candidate ids belong (sender) and gave no addressee. The commands are one imperative group, imp2, so it is the part rather than cl2 and cl3 separately. cl4 and cl5 remain parts of the speech.
groups.category: speech with addressee and nested commands

groups.why: One command, 'pray to the LORD', with its aim, that he remove the frogs. The builder used 'part', which is not a role of the imperative kind. 'aim' is the role for what a command is for.
cl3 is the aim of the command in imp2, not a command, so the builder's second command is wrong. cl4 is a promise (cohortative), not a command, so there is no command for this group to hold.
groups.category: group made from a purpose clause

groups.why: cl4 is Pharaoh's promise, not a command. The purpose of letting go, cl5, is carried by the purpose link from cl4, not by an imperative group.

cant_tell.what: Whether cl4 (I will let the people go) is conditional on the removal in cl3, as in 'if he removes the frogs, then I will let them go'.
cant_tell.why: The waw is plain and the Hebrew marks no condition. The 'if' link would need the form to carry the condition, and it does not, so the plain 'and' is kept.

cant_tell.what: Whether the purpose link applies from cl4 to cl5 when the first clause is a cohortative rather than a command.
cant_tell.why: The purpose type's text names a command as the first term. The sense (release for the sacrifice) is plain, so purpose is added, but the type's wording does not cover a cohortative first term.
